title: Descriptive Statistics: Measures of Centre and Spread

blocks.text: Imagine you have a dataset of the ages of people attending a tech conference. How would you summarize this data to understand the typical age and its variability?

blocks.markdown: Descriptive statistics provide a way to summarize and describe the essential features of a dataset. In this lesson, we will explore measures of central tendency and dispersion, which help us understand the data's center and spread.

blocks.title: Measures of Central Tendency
blocks.text: The mean, median, and mode are measures of central tendency that describe the center of a dataset.

blocks.caption: The mean is the sum of all data points divided by the number of data points.

blocks.markdown: The median is the middle value when the data is ordered. If the dataset has an even number of observations, the median is the average of the two middle numbers.

blocks.title: Mode
blocks.text: The mode is the value that appears most frequently in a dataset. A dataset may have one mode, more than one mode, or no mode at all.

blocks.markdown: Measures of spread provide insight into the variability of the data. Common measures include variance, standard deviation, and interquartile range (IQR).

blocks.caption: Variance measures the average squared deviation from the mean.

blocks.title: Interquartile Range (IQR)
blocks.text: The IQR is the difference between the third quartile (Q3) and the first quartile (Q1) and measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data.

blocks.title: Calculating the Mean and Median
blocks.prompt: Consider the dataset: [3, 7, 8, 5, 12, 14, 21, 13, 18]. Calculate the mean and median.

steps.text: To find the mean, sum all the numbers and divide by the count of numbers.
To find the median, first order the data: [3, 5, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14, 18, 21]. The median is the middle value.

blocks.answer: The mean is 11.22 and the median is 12.

blocks.markdown: Outliers are data points that differ significantly from other observations. They can be identified using various methods, one of which involves the interquartile range (IQR).

blocks.title: Identifying Outliers
blocks.text: A common rule is that any data point more than 1.5 times the IQR above the third quartile or below the first quartile is considered an outlier.

blocks.title: Identifying Outliers
blocks.prompt: Given the dataset: [10, 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 18, 19, 29], identify any outliers.

steps.text: First, find Q1 and Q3. Order the data: [10, 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 18, 19, 29]. Q1 is the median of the first half: 13. Q3 is the median of the second half: 18.
Calculate the IQR: IQR = Q3 - Q1 = 18 - 13 = 5.
Determine the outlier thresholds: Lower bound = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR = 13 - 7.5 = 5.5. Upper bound = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR = 18 + 7.5 = 25.5.
Identify outliers: Any value below 5.5 or above 25.5 is an outlier. Here, 29 is an outlier.

blocks.answer: The outlier in the dataset is 29.

blocks.markdown: In some cases, the median provides a better summary of a dataset than the mean, especially when the data contains outliers or is skewed.

blocks.title: When to Use the Median
blocks.text: If a dataset includes extreme values, the mean can be misleading. The median, being the middle value, is less affected by outliers and skewed data.

points: The mean, median, and mode are key measures of central tendency.
Variance and IQR are important measures of data spread.
Outliers can be identified using the 1.5 * IQR rule.
The median is robust to outliers and skewed data.
